and seven days thereafter the house at Velsen and the fluyt Soetendael, Soetendael being entirely unloaded for sale, and Spanbroeck and the house at Velsen had their cargo transported with our hookers [small trading vessels] to Colombo. The inventory of these same three ships' cargoes is enclosed herewith. With the same we have indeed received Your Excellency's pleasant and highly esteemed letters of the 24th and August, together with extracts concerning the matter of Ceylon and subordinate places from the general letters written by Your Excellency on the 9th of May and 24th of August of the past year to my Lords the Governor General and Council of India, just as we have also subsequently received by the overland route from Persia the copies of the aforementioned extracts and the original letters written by Your Excellency to the respective governors and directors of these regions on the 9th of May and 24th of August. The receipt of the particular letters from the Chambers of Amsterdam and Middelburgh has been answered here by their Excellencies each individually. In order to serve Your Excellency with a response to the two aforementioned extracts of the 9th and 24th of August of the past year, we shall, following Your Excellency's regulation, begin with Tanara, reporting the latest news that has come to us from Commander Hendrik van Reede and council at Cochin, dated the 29th of October last, that the annulment of the pepper contract by the court merchant Narnamaloe had been accepted, but the same had not proceeded so easily, or rather the aforementioned Maloe had been the cause that the Company had not approved it at Batavia, as he according to his account had been promised. We can very well believe that the under-merchant De Bruijn will have overstepped himself in this work with unnecessary and unlawful words, as can be clearly measured from his written reports and letters, and particularly that one has been very hasty in all this work, even without ever having received from us

--- CHUNK 2 ---
had the Company been the cause that it had not been approved by their Excellencies at Batavia, as he according to his account had been promised. We can very well believe that the under-merchant De Bruijn will have overstepped himself in this work with unnecessary and unlawful words, as can be clearly measured from his written reports and letters, and particularly that one has been very hasty in all this work, even without ever having received from us or their Excellencies at Batavia any order to do so, and in this way the Company is often led into trouble by the ignorance and poor judgment of its servants. What our opinion concerning the aforementioned De Bruijn may be, you will find set forth in our last letter dated the 1st of September from Punto Pedro or Paritature to their Excellencies at Batavia, and upon which we await their Excellencies' order in January next. It has seemed to us very suspicious, the great difficulty which this man has always made in order to annul this contract, which we nevertheless have never been able to see, as Your Excellency has become clear from our previous letters, both to Batavia as well as to Your Excellency at length, and now also with reasons by the Honorable Van Reede writing to the under-merchant Da Bruijn it is confirmed that he has not only in no way upheld the Company's right concerning the made contract, but has rather striven to place the Company in the wrong, and that anyone reading such daily registers would not be able to judge otherwise than that the Company had dealt unreasonably with the Nayak, or otherwise (as such would also be our express opinion) that the Company's servants themselves conduct such matters in order to force their masters to that which the servants are inclined to and find advantageous, and further such more as Your Excellency in the letter of the aforementioned Honorable

--- CHUNK 3 ---
has rather striven to place the Company in the wrong, and that anyone reading such daily registers would not be able to judge otherwise than that the Company had dealt unreasonably with the Nayak, or otherwise (as such would also be our express opinion) that the Company's servants themselves conduct such matters in order to force their masters to that which the servants are inclined to and find advantageous, and further such more as Your Excellency in the letter of the aforementioned Honorable Van Reede of the 30th of August to the Resident De Bruijn will find set forth in detail. The Company's greatest interest concerning the lands of Canara seems to consist in that we, through the annulment of the contract, now remain deprived of our right to the export of wild cinnamon, which will now be exported by the French and English as well as by us. But since the same cinnamon is of very little value, and we can purchase it as well as others under the hand as well as publicly, we hope that the damage from this will be less than to purchase pepper at such a high price, and that our competing merchants will gain so little profit on the Canara pepper (which is mostly purchased for cash) that their desire for the one and the other will cool somewhat, particularly if we through steady purchase of a reasonable quantity of pepper in Canara take care that the price does not fall below 6 stuivers [small Dutch coins] per pound or 48 rixdollars [modern equivalent: Dutch currency] per candil [a measure of weight] of 470 pounds, and that we prevent the wild cinnamon from being exported sometimes through gifts and sometimes through purchase as much as we are able. How our concept concerning that work has been situated is evident to Your Excellency in various of our previous letters, in which, since we are hindered by the change of times, we shall now do our best to

--- CHUNK 4 ---
take care that the price does not fall below 6 stuivers per pound or 48 rixdollars per candil of 470 pounds, and that we prevent the wild cinnamon from being exported sometimes through gifts and sometimes through purchase as much as we are able. How our concept concerning that work has been situated is evident to Your Excellency in various of our previous letters, in which, since we are hindered by the change of times, we shall now do our best to manage ourselves, and look after the Company's interest. Regarding Tananoor, the state of affairs at Cananoor you will find set forth very extensively in the letters from Commander Hendrik van Reede and the council at Cochin dated the 15th of August and 29th of October last and written to their Excellencies at Batavia and sent to us in copy. In which Your Excellency it appears how vigorously our European neighbors labor to establish their trade in their corner, and how the Malabar Zamorin or the prince Rammenetri knows how to draw his advantage from this, and openly violates the contract made with us. Whereas Adersia, the chief of the Moors, finding no taste in this for himself, seems to hold our side to his profit in order to maintain the Company's reputation and his credit, and not to lose entirely his Moorish and Persian trade. For now that pepper is being driven up so high in this turmoil, his profits must necessarily be less. What our opinion concerning this matter may be, you will find set forth in our letters to Batavia and in our letters dated the 23rd of July and the 7th of September sent off, namely that we shall no longer involve ourselves in this work with protests, but shall see to everything, purchasing with the others the pepper according to market price so that everyone may find pepper dear, through which means we shall possess the greatest peace, and also

--- CHUNK 5 ---
his profits must necessarily be less. What our opinion concerning this matter may be, you will find set forth in our letters to Batavia and in our letters dated the 23rd of July and the 7th of September sent off, namely that we shall no longer involve ourselves in this work with protests, but shall see to everything, purchasing with the others the pepper according to market price so that everyone may find pepper dear, through which means we shall possess the greatest peace, and also (in our judgment) no lesser advantages, and whereby on the other hand the Malabar Zamorin will labor all the more to be favored by the English and French, and us in turn to remain more favorably disposed toward us for our forbearance. Whereas between this the trade of Adersia falling in, one may hope that the others will soon grow weary and proceed of their own accord. Also it seems to us for now still very inadvisable to molest these nations in Indian waters, so as not to entice them also to South Malabar, where they could cause us greater trouble and damage. We further conduct ourselves toward our aforementioned Batavian and Malabar letters with all respect. Regarding the Samorin, with the Samorin we had hoped in the past good season to have made a good even reckoning, but various accidents have hindered us therein, of which in this matter (omitting the extent) we conduct ourselves toward the letters concerning that matter written to their Excellencies at Batavia, and especially toward the report made by Major Joan Bax with confirmation not only from all the war officers but even the common soldiers publicly thereupon, the aforementioned report here enclosed in copy. Whether now their Excellencies at Batavia will still be able to second us in January next with a good number of war troops, time must tell. In any case it must be held without doubt that without forcing the Samorin we shall never have peace.

--- CHUNK 1 ---
and especially in a Report by Major Joan Bax [uncertain: possibly "Joan Bax" or similar name] with confirmation not only from all the military officers but even from the common soldiers publicly made thereupon, the aforementioned report herewith in Copy or now—Your Excellencies in Batavia [Batavia: modern Jakarta] will still be able to support us in January next with a good number of military forces; time must tell. In any case, it must undoubtedly be held that we can never expect peace on Malabar [Malabar: southwestern coast of India] without forcing the Samorin [Samorin: Hindu ruler of Calicut], for the hope which Your Excellencies in Batavia had for a good Peace has not followed, and will also never be obtained without weapons or at least without fear of them. Let anyone judge of this as he will, for Your Excellencies can easily see that the right of the King of Cochin [Cochin: Portuguese/Dutch colonial possession in India] necessarily requires the restitution of his lands, which were treacherously taken from him by the Samorin during his previous misfortune for his restoration, and since the entire security of our trade and the Company's interest with this Raja of Cochin depends upon this restoration, as the Raja is our protector, both justice and necessity make it clear that we are obliged to maintain the Raja of Cochin in his rightful claim. Besides this restitution of lands, the Company's own interest requires the firm possession of Oranganoor [Oranganoor: fortified position] in order to bind the Samorin to his word and promises with this pledge and to keep it, just as Oranganoor was also handed over to him on no other condition with half of the cannon and delivered into his hand, as can sufficiently be seen from the surrender document, and so if anyone now thinks that the Samorin with fair words or through persuasion of anyone's rightful judgment will give up such great advantages, he will too late discover how far his unfounded hope has deceived him.

If we now still receive military force, we do not see the chance worsened. Yes, we would still have all the hope that everything could be accomplished without bloodshed, since Your Excellencies' weapons (thank God) are so well known among the Malabaris that no one will dare to wait for them, and even less to test them. It is also certain that if it could be obtained through another means than weapons, it would have been settled long ago. We must also testify that the Van Reede has shown very great diligence in accommodating the work toward peace without weapons, but the deed has shown that His Excellency has done this more to make you and

Being present on Malabar from the Ceylonese militia a captain, 4 lieutenants, three ensigns and 270 common soldiers, without which there would be very little strength there, with which force joined to the Malabar militia His Excellency has now advanced so far that there is great hope of destroying the Cranganoor [Cranganoor: fortified position] heathen tower and pagoda with cannon. If this succeeds, Your Excellencies will see such great advantage as is expressed in His Excellency's aforementioned last letter of the 29th of October, the expansion of Cotjaer [Cotjaer: fortified position] and Battecalo [Battecalo: fortified position], and the revolt that has occurred in the Colombo lands deprives us of the means to assist His Excellency further with Cochin, and if we receive no help from Batavia, it will be impossible for us to send more assistance there, having ourselves the borrowed militia in the highest need, as it is now becoming clear that the Malabar separation brings no advantage to the Company. The state and situation of the city and lands of Cochin and especially of the Raja are so well extended in the letter of the 15th of August.

--- CHUNK 1 ---
us the means to assist Cochin further, and if we receive no help from Batavia, it will be impossible for us to deploy further assistance there, having ourselves great need of our borrowed militia. As it now becomes clear that the Malabar separation brings no advantage to the Company, the state and situation of the city and lands of Cochin and particularly of the Raja are so extensively detailed in the letter of the 15th of August [15 August] attached herewith in duplicate copy that we would not know what to add to it. And Your Excellency may now see in that same letter how necessary it was that we took the Malabar land administration upon ourselves for the King, which he can now well maintain, whereas otherwise he would certainly have been ruined and gone to ruin entirely. Many other matters that were so vigorously driven against us by the previous two last Commanders are here not only explained but so clarified that Your Excellency can now easily judge the difference. It is to be wished that it had pleased God that we could have employed this man as Commander, as we so earnestly requested, for then all those altercations would not have occurred, and without all doubt the Company would have been better served. And since we wrote in our letter dated the eleventh of September to Batavia, we have confirmed ourselves with the aforementioned letter of the 15th of August as the principal [document], and in the Malabar letter the entire state of the lands of Dorca, Calcoilan, Cattembali, Marta, Coilan, Tengenapatan, and Trevancor [Travancore] is well and carefully detailed. And we also still await further advice from Your Excellency from Malabar to send along with this, so we shall — here end the Malabar matter and hereafter add what with the arrival of the aforesaid Malabar advice may still be necessary. Madure [Madura] the state

--- CHUNK 2 ---
15th of August as the principal [document], and in the Malabar letter the entire state of the lands of Dorca, Calcoilan, Cattembali, Marta, Coilan, Tengenapatan, and Trevancor [Travancore] is well and carefully detailed. And we also still await further advice from Your Excellency from Malabar to send along with this, so we shall — here end the Malabar matter and hereafter add what with the arrival of the aforesaid Malabar advice may still be necessary. Madure [Madura] the state and situation in the lands of Tuticorin and Madura is now, thank God, brought into good peace and tranquility. But to our sorrow, the promised shipment to the Nayak [Nayak: regional ruler] has not been able to proceed because in sending the projected gift, the very best tusked elephant has died, just the day before the boat the Dolphin arrived at Tuticorin. The loss of this fine beast (being worth no less than 3,000 Rixdollars [modern equivalent: approximately 3,000 Dutch guilders]) has grieved us until now, because among the many captured [elephants], we have not been able to obtain such a one. We expect the Honorable Laurens Pijl from Tuticorin to come here so that we may form the gift in his Honorable hands and have it sent without delay with firm hope that we shall obtain our objective well and obtain from the Nayak not only free and unencumbered trade in all his lands but also such firm establishment and residence for our exchange as Your Excellency is shown by a separate map attached hereto, which is depicted on the Hook as a new residence, a costly situation and much better situated than the old lodge, of which Your Excellency in the letter dated 23 July to Batavia will see our sentiment more clearly. This peaceful state now gives us great occasion to continue our trade, which at present is found to be so considerable that we in few

--- CHUNK 3 ---
exchange as Your Excellency is shown by a separate map attached hereto, which is depicted on the Hook as a new residence, a costly situation and much better situated than the old lodge, of which Your Excellency in the letter dated 23 July to Batavia will see our sentiment more clearly. This peaceful state now gives us great occasion to continue our trade, which at present is found to be so considerable that we hope in few years to excuse Coromandel entirely, and moreover for the fatherland and Persia there shall still remain something left over. Now going with these ships we are packing various sorts of cloths, namely packs of salempuris [type of cloth], fine moris [type of cloth], guinea linen, just as everything is more clearly and specifically detailed in the invoice. Now please Your Excellency be mindful that our reduction of Coromandel differs 15 stuivers [modern equivalent: small Dutch coins] on every pagoda [pagoda: Indian gold coin] or 7½ on every Rixdollar [Rixdollar: currency], making two and a half stuivers on every guilder, and thus 12½ guilders on hundred guilders, so that the purchase is brought in the invoice dearer than on Coromandel, where (above the profit on the gold in the minting of the pagodas obtained) the pagoda is valued at only 105 stuivers. Which considerable difference being deducted, Your Excellency will find that our Madura cloths in quality do not fall short of the Coromandel ones, yet will fall at better price. All our effort shall we apply to obtaining privilege from the Madura court to mint coins at Tuticorin just as now happens at Palliacatte [Paliacate], so that such Madura pagodas and fanums [fanam: small Indian coin] then with the Palliacatte ones in value and alloy equally set and according to ratio justly valued, could also be made current on Ceylon [Sri Lanka] to great benefit of the inhabitants and not less to the furtherance of trade. Almighty God we beseech to grant his gracious blessing hereto, and that we may obtain the same from the

--- CHUNK 4 ---
court to mint coins at Tuticorin just as now happens at Palliacatte [Paliacate], so that such Madura pagodas and fanums [fanam: small Indian coin] then with the Palliacatte ones in value and alloy equally set and according to ratio justly valued, could also be made current on Ceylon [Sri Lanka] to great benefit of the inhabitants and not less to the furtherance of trade. Almighty God we beseech to grant his gracious blessing hereto, and that we may obtain the same from the Nayak of Madura, as we reckon that the Company would profit yearly a considerable amount from it. Now that we through God's grace have placed the entire coast of the island of Ceylon as well as all harbors principally under our power, we lack nothing but Your Excellency or their Excellencies from Batavia [Batavia: Jakarta] positive orders to proceed with our design and concept and to keep off Ceylon all Moors and private traders who are harmful to us and even to bring to nothing all that the Singhalese and inhabitants of this island shall need. We shall never have rest on Ceylon, of which before now enough and so much has been written that we could not add to it in this [letter], that which is not declared in our previous [letters]. Your Excellency we specially request to read our letter dated the 23rd July sent to their Excellencies to Batavia, wherein Your Excellency will find cited that Ceylon can yearly consume 500,000 stuivers [modern equivalent: small Dutch coins] worth of catechu [catechu: astringent extract from betel nut], and in return can deliver 3,000 lasts [last: unit of weight/volume] of areca [areca: betel nut], truly a trade that well merits to be laid to heart. So if we now keep the purchase and sale of the cloths and areca under our power, can easily be made clear what advantages are to be expected from it and to be hoped for, and which we would already tax at some tons of gold yearly, for as long as we have the Moors on Ceylon to hope for

--- CHUNK 5 ---
consume 500,000 stuivers [modern equivalent: small Dutch coins] worth of catechu [catechu: astringent extract from betel nut], and in return can deliver 3,000 lasts [last: unit of weight/volume] of areca [areca: betel nut], truly a trade that well merits to be laid to heart. So if we now keep the purchase and sale of the cloths and areca under our power, can easily be made clear what advantages are to be expected from it and to be hoped for, and which we would already tax at some tons of gold yearly, for as long as we have the Moors on Ceylon to hope for, we shall also not obtain our objective, for on Madura the cloths jointly with the Moors being purchased, the matter speaks for itself that they will adulterate the cloths and know how to see all advantage for themselves above all, before the same can also not otherwise be expected in the sale on Ceylon and in the purchase and sale of the areca, as well on Ceylon as on the coasts of Madura and Coromandel. With this revolt in the lands of Colombo that has occurred, a most excellent opportunity is given to us to make a beginning, of which Your Excellency in the Colombo matter our considerations and the right that we believe we have thereto will be declared at length, and to which we shall refer in the continuation of this matter. Although our present lodge at Tuticorin by the presence of the Honorable van Goens there was already placed in fairly good defense according to the times and was provided with 24 pieces of cannon for defense, yet such could only happen with erected palisades from within with earth brought up, which beginning to rot in the ground, we now shall have to think first of reforming those, to rebuild our fortification in stone. We have received no small joy that Your Excellency have finally been pleased to resolve, even against the will of the Nayak, to establish ourselves firmly there. The great necessity shows itself so on all sides that we believe by now to see it

--- CHUNK 1 ---
constructed with upright palisades on the inside filled with earth, which beginning to rot in the ground, we shall now at the earliest have to think about replacing them, in order to rebuild our fortification in stone. It has been no small joy to us that Your Excellencies have finally been pleased to resolve to establish ourselves firmly there against the will of the Nayak [local ruler], the great necessity showing itself so clearly on all sides that we believe it would be a great oversight to delay, and although Their Excellencies at Batavia [Jakarta] seem to restrict us somewhat again in this matter, we nevertheless hope to conduct the matter in such a way that Their Excellencies and Your Excellencies will be satisfied, and we shall nevertheless carry out our intention. The meeting between the Honorable van Goens and the Stadthouder Barmilappa Pulle you will find recounted in our daily register kept at Tuticorin [Thoothukudi] regarding this matter and attached separately in extract herewith, in which joint discussion the matter of fortification was discussed at length and (as the deed now shows:) has removed a great part of the distrust that previously possessed the hearts of these people and especially of this heathen toll-collector Barmilappa Pulle, laying down our intention to hold the present lodge in defense for so long until we shall be able to transport ourselves into the new residence, so that we can then direct all matters there so that Tuticorin may in time come within its walls and we shall be able to secure a good number of weavers from all tyranny, to which poor people are now subject, as Your Excellencies in our letters regarding Goijlant, the Court of Breda, and concerning Coromandel dated the 30th of May, 23rd of July, 11th of September of this year, written and thereafter sent to Their Excellencies at Batavia, will be pleased to see, for in order to keep all Europeans out of the inlet of

--- CHUNK 2 ---
to direct all matters there so that Tuticorin may in time come within its walls and we shall be able to secure a good number of weavers from all tyranny, to which poor people are now subject, as Your Excellencies in our letters regarding Goijlant, the Court of Breda, and concerning Coromandel dated the 30th of May, 23rd of July, 11th of September of this year, written and thereafter sent to Their Excellencies at Batavia, will be pleased to see, for in order to keep all Europeans out of the inlet of Ceylon [Sri Lanka] is the service of the Esteemed Company of the highest importance, because beyond the profits therein the peace on this island will greatly depend, and although we are at present empowered by a valid contract to keep all Europeans out of the inlet, such will not be achieved with tranquility until our good right is secured by a suitable fortress, we shall apply all management not only to the sea but also to peace and thus endeavor to take Your Excellencies' praiseworthy order and maxims in the highest regard, to which may Almighty God be pleased to grant His blessing. Regarding the matter that we have seen in Your Excellencies' missive concerning the purchase of pearls, we fear we shall have to meet with difficulties again, as after the examination of the banks in March last no suitable shells were found that could have borne the costs of an ordinary pearl fishery, and this both at Tuticorin and before Arippo [Arippu] or Manaar [Mannar], being according to the reports made to us the old shells either covered with sand or gaping, which then as we are told their pearls fall out or are thrown away. Young shells were in great abundance on both banks but which would not be suitable for another 2 years, meanwhile we nevertheless find that the Moors make their work the whole year through (even in the bad season:) to

--- CHUNK 3 ---
before Arippo or Manaar, being according to the reports made to us the old shells either covered with sand or gaping, which then as we are told their pearls fall out or are thrown away. Young shells were in great abundance on both banks but which would not be suitable for another 2 years, meanwhile we nevertheless find that the Moors make their work the whole year through (even in the bad season:) to work the banks roughly and extensively, which we shall henceforth have to prevent with defensive sailing vessels and rowing boats. Until now we have been very scrupulous about punishing such pearl robbers (: following the example of the Portuguese :) with death, those who were caught at it, which if it does not happen this thievery will never cease, these Moors having the land of the Teuver [Tanjore/Thanjavur] as their refuge, which also protects them and resists correction, so that we shall henceforth have to make it our duty to pursue these thieves at sea and forthwith punish them with the rope so that death follows, of which we shall first have a placard published again on all harbors of the Teuver and Madure [Madurai], but although we had received a good sum of money from the pearl fishery in the year before last, it was nevertheless impossible for us to spend the required 1006 guilders, as we now again just as in the year before last sit without money, having had to draw 25,000 pagodas [modern equivalent: a monetary unit] from Paliacatte [Pulicat] to save ourselves, from where we may now perhaps receive help in money, since there is nothing left over there and whereby we are at present in no small difficulty, having scarcely money to pay the faithful soldiers and other monthly personnel their wages and to meet other unavoidable expenses, no money having come to us from Batavia, Persia, or Suratte [Surat], and the payment consisting of 406 guilders with

--- CHUNK 4 ---
from Paliacatte 25,000 pagodas to save ourselves, from where we may now perhaps receive help in money, since there is nothing left over there and whereby we are at present in no small difficulty, having scarcely money to pay the faithful soldiers and other monthly personnel their wages and to meet other unavoidable expenses, no money having come to us from Batavia, Persia, or Suratte, and the payment consisting of 406 guilders with the Poles at the house at Velsen &c. received has already been consumed. Whether we shall hold a fishery in March next at Manaar or Tuticorin will be advised to Your Excellencies by the next land [dispatch]. As our trade at Tuticorin and in the lands of Madure is becoming of such great importance, we have hope that by suppressing the Moors we shall be able to gather and purchase our necessary goods in the lands of Madure, Travancore [Trivandrum] &c. ourselves, Your Excellencies can easily judge that we shall need greater capital (at least for the first :) especially if we shall make purchases for Persia, Basra [Basrah], and further the Fatherland [Netherlands], in order to obtain the mouries [a type of cloth] and salempouris [a type of cloth] on the breadth according to the patriot's demand will at first be the greatest difficulty, being otherwise (in our judgment:) especially the Guinea linen cloth better in cloth and thread than the Coromandel linen, Your Excellencies accordingly humbly requesting that we may be supported with more capital to favor this new opening trade. We have requested Their Excellencies at Batavia to keep the Moors from here with the best means to be devised for this, which we hope will be permitted to us, or otherwise we see no chance to achieve our objective (: which nevertheless the Company holds in such high regard :), which exclusion of the Moors having succeeded would then our speculation fall well, in order to hold the areca [betel nut] alone also under the Company's power
